Precision reduction reduces the memory footprint, as well as speeds up computation by reducing the data transfer needs between the memory and the compute units of the GPUs. Most neural networks are memory-bandwidth constrained and so the conversion of FP32 to FP16 to INT8 (including a halving or quartering both activations and weights) enables GPUs to perform more data per cycle. This is enhanced by Tensor Cores who perform multiple low-precision matrix multiplications at the same time, as opposed to a single one at a time as with old CUDA cores.

This implies that a single Tensor Core can do multiple fused multiply-accumulate (FMA) operations in a single clock, increasing throughput whilst retaining almost FP32 accuracy. The smaller types of data also enhance usage of cache and shared memory, which decreases the latency and energy used.

## Inference Frameworks on Different Hardware

Due to the different instructions and optimizations available on each hardware when quantizing a neural network, specific libraries are available to exploit this:

1. **NVIDIA TensorRT:** The high-performance deep learning inference optimizer by NVIDIA, optimized to run on NVIDIA GPUs. It feeds trained models (via frameworks such as TensorFlow or PyTorch, typically by exporting to ONNX) and compiles a highly optimized runtime engine by using methods such as layer fusion, precision calibration and using Tensor Cores.
2. **AMD MIGraphX:** MIGraphX is a graph compiler and runtime in AMD ROCm software stack to execute inference on AMD Radeon/Instinct GPUs (and CPUs) by acceleration. It does graph optimizations and can run low-precision programs on AMD hardware.
3. **Intel OpenVINO:** Intel’s open inference toolkit support on Intel CPUs, GPUs and VPUs. It translates models into an Intermediate Representation (IR) and applies hardware-specific compiler optimizations to each target device.
4. **ONNX Runtime (ORT):** Open-source cross-platform inference engine capable of executing ONNX models on many hardware platforms. ONNX Runtime can be run on CPUs, GPUs and accelerators and may use any of many execution providers such as calling TensorRT on NVIDIA GPUs, oneDNN (MKL-DNN) on CPUs, MIGraphX on AMD GPUs, OpenVINO on Intel, CoreML on Apple, etc. This renders it a universal solution to implement quantized models on any device.

## NVIDIA TensorRT

TensorRT is the NVIDIA library that runs deep learning models on GPUs in the most efficient way possible. TensorRT is often referred to as an inference optimizer or deep learning compiler which takes a trained model and optimizes it to the target GPU to produce an engine that is much faster than the original model. It does so by a range of graph-level and kernel-level optimizations, including layer fusion, kernel auto-tuning, precision selection and optimized memory reuse. Consequently, models running on TensorRT can typically run 2x-4x faster than their FP32 equivalents.

The main advantage of TensorRT is the possibility to use Tensor Cores and mixed-precision calculation to make inferences faster. Tensor Cores are special hardware units, present in Volta, Turing, Ampere and later NVIDIA architectures, which execute a type of matrix multiply-accumulate at lower precision formats, including FP16, INT8 or even FP8.

Practically, FP16 inference can achieve up to a 2x speed improvement with a small loss in accuracy since it does not change the floating-point representation, just uses fewer bits. This ensures that models can frequently be executed at half precision without retraining, in contrast to INT8 quantization which usually must either be calibrated or trained with quantization awareness.

### FP16 Optimization in TensorRT

Activating FP16 in TensorRT is easy. In constructing an engine, we just enable FP16 precision by setting the builder configuration flag to True. In the Python API, this can be done as follows:

> import tensorrt as trt
>
> logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.INFO)
>
> builder = trt.Builder(logger)
>
> network = builder.create\_network(flags=1 << int(trt.NetworkDefinitionCreationFlag.EXPLICIT\_BATCH))
>
> config = builder.create\_builder\_config()
>
> if builder.platform\_has\_fast\_fp16:
>
> config.set\_flag(trt.BuilderFlag.FP16)
>
> engine = builder.build\_engine(network, config)

TensorRT will then optimize the network automatically and selectively run layers and operations that can run safely in FP16, leaving any numerically sensitive or incompatible layers to run in FP32. This is a mixed-precision implementation that will provide the highest possible speedup but not accuracy.

In this optimization, TensorRT introduces a number of internal transformations:

- It combines compatible layers to reduce data transfers and kernel launches.
- It picks the most optimized FP16 Tensor Core kernels of the convolutions and the matrix multiplications.
- It recycles activation buffers to minimize the memory footprint in the GPU.

The end result is an FP16 or mixed-precision engine that is optimized to the particular architecture of the GPU.

### FP16 Support and Benefits

When a model is run in FP16 mode on the above mentioned GPUs architecture, the Tensor Cores will do half-precision matrix multiplication and accumulate the result in higher precision which maintains both speed and number accuracy. In comparison, previous architectures like Pascal (GTX 10-series, Tesla P4/P40) lack Tensor Cores and therefore cannot execute FP16 with equivalent acceleration but can support FP16 math at lower throughput on standard CUDA cores.

FP16 precision not only increases the speed of computation but also cuts the amount of memory used in half, as each element in a tensor takes 2 bytes as opposed to 4. The result is smaller model sizes, quicker data transfers and greater use of cache & bandwidth. These bandwidth savings can save overall latency and power usage because many deep learning workloads are memory-bound, not compute-bound. Inference on FP16, therefore, provides a trade-off of accuracy, speed and efficiency particularly in inference at scale or real-time.

Though FP16 is usually almost as accurate as FP32, numerical differences may arise because 16-bit floating-point numbers have a small dynamic range. TensorRT manages to reduce these effects by automatically retaining sensitive operations in full precision. To ensure maximum accuracy, NVIDIA suggests checking inference results following conversion to FP16 and fine-tuning the model may be optional in case the application is especially sensitive to differences in accuracy.

## ONNX Runtime: Portable Quantized Inference Across Platforms

ONNX Runtime (ORT) is a high-performance inference engine able to infer models in the ONNX format on a wide range of hardware platforms efficiently. Microsoft established it as a single runtime layer that exposes hardware details, you can convert your trained model (PyTorch, TensorFlow, etc.) to ONNX once and then execute it anywhere (CPU, GPU, mobile, edge) by simply selecting the correct Execution Provider (EP). Execution Providers are the backends that enable ORT to take advantage of certain accelerators:

- **CUDA EP:** Executes CUDA kernels on NVIDIA GPUs (FP32 and FP16)
- **TensorRT EP:** Executes the models in NVIDIA TensorRT to achieve the highest performance (FP16, INT8, etc.)
- **OpenVINO EP:** OpenVINO is optimized to run on Intel CPUs, iGPUs and VPUs.
- **DirectML, MIGraphX, CoreML,** etc. are aimed at other hardware.

This is a modular EP system and you do not have to modify your model or inference code, simply select a provider that fits your specific device and ORT will run optimally with that provider.

### Converting a Model to FP16

When your model is trained in FP32 or exported in FP32, it is easily converted to FP16 with the ONNX runtime conversion tool. This transforms tensors and operators where it is possible to use the float16 data type.

> import onnx
>
> from onnxconverter\_common import float16
>
> model = onnx.load(“path/to/model.onnx”)
>
> model\_fp16 = float16.convert\_float\_to\_float16(model)
>
> onnx.save(model\_fp16, “path/to/model\_fp16.onnx”)

This script will rewrite your model using FP16 weights and operations without modifying unsupported layers and automatically converting it to a mixed-precision model.

### Executing FP16 Models on GPU

When you have a half-precision model, you can execute it with ONNX Runtime using the CUDA or TensorRT Execution Providers.

**With the CUDA Execution Provider:**

> import onnxruntime as ort
>
> sess = ort.InferenceSession( “modelfp16.onnx”, providers=\[“CUDAExecutionProvider”\] )

The CUDA EP also supports FP32 and FP16 computation. When you feed tensors of FP16 as input, ORT will automatically execute compatible operations in FP16, using CUDA native half-precision kernels.

In order to be as efficient as possible:

- The inputs must be given as np.float16.
- The ONNX model operations must be able to use FP16 (ORT will default to FP32).

**With the TensorRT Execution Provider:**

> import onnxruntime as ort
>
> sess = ort.InferenceSession( “modelfp16.onnx”, providers=\[“TensorrtExecutionProvider”, “CUDAExecutionProvider”\] )

The TensorRT EP is more optimized. ORT takes the ONNX graph under the hood and compiles it into a more optimized engine with help of TensorRT. With FP16 (enabled by default when your GPU supports it) turned on, TensorRT can fuse layers, run FP16 Tensor Cores and restructure operations to keep memory and compute overheads to a minimum.

## Conclusion

FP16 accuracy has become one of the most efficient methods to enable deep learning inference with no detail of complete quantization. Mixed-precision arithmetic renders a substantial performance improvement with modern NVIDIA GPUs, equipped with Tensor Cores designed to execute half-precision arithmetic, with close-to-FP32 accuracy. Today, we discussed the potential of FP16 to enable faster and more memory efficient inference, especially when implemented using frameworks such as NVIDIA TensorRT and ONNX Runtime. TensorRT provides highest performance on NVIDIA devices by automatically converting compatible layers to FP16 and fusing operations to perform on the Tensor Cores, with common 2–4x speed improvements over FP32. Meanwhile, ONNX Runtime provides a unified, cross-platform inference layer that can use FP16 using both the CUDA and TensorRT Execution Providers to enable mixed-precision inference with minimal effort. These tools collectively enable the optimization of FP16 to be a realistic and highly efficient approach to deploy deep learning models with enhanced performance and scalability.

I was comparing the inference times for an input using pytorch and onnxruntime and I find that onnxruntime is actually slower on GPU while being significantly faster on CPU

I was tryng this on Windows 10.

- ONNX Runtime installed from source - ONNX Runtime version: 1.11.0 (onnx version 1.10.1)
- Python version - 3.8.12
- CUDA/cuDNN version - cuda version 11.5, cudnn version 8.2
- GPU model and memory - Quadro M2000M, 4 GB

**Relevant code -**

```
import torch
from torchvision import models
import onnxruntime    # to inference ONNX models, we use the ONNX Runtime
import onnx
import os
import time

batch_size = 1
total_samples = 1000
device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

def convert_to_onnx(resnet):
   resnet.eval()
   dummy_input = (torch.randn(batch_size, 3, 224, 224, device=device)).to(device=device)
   input_names = [ 'input' ]
   output_names = [ 'output' ]
   torch.onnx.export(resnet,
               dummy_input,
               "resnet18.onnx",
               verbose=True,
               opset_version=13,
               input_names=input_names,
               output_names=output_names,
               export_params=True,
               do_constant_folding=True,
               dynamic_axes={
                  'input': {0: 'batch_size'},  # variable length axes
                  'output': {0: 'batch_size'}}
               )

def infer_pytorch(resnet):
   print('Pytorch Inference')
   print('==========================')
   print()

   x = torch.randn((batch_size, 3, 224, 224))
   x = x.to(device=device)

   latency = []
   for i in range(total_samples):
      t0 = time.time()
      resnet.eval()
      with torch.no_grad():
         out = resnet(x)
      latency.append(time.time() - t0)

   print('Number of runs:', len(latency))
   print("Average PyTorch {} Inference time = {} ms".format(device.type, format(sum(latency) * 1000 / len(latency), '.2f')))

def to_numpy(tensor):
   return tensor.detach().cpu().numpy() if tensor.requires_grad else tensor.cpu().numpy()

def infer_onnxruntime():
   print('Onnxruntime Inference')
   print('==========================')
   print()

   onnx_model = onnx.load("resnet18.onnx")
   onnx.checker.check_model(onnx_model)

   # Input
   x = torch.randn((batch_size, 3, 224, 224))
   x = x.to(device=device)
   x = to_numpy(x)

   so = onnxruntime.SessionOptions()
   so.execution_mode = onnxruntime.ExecutionMode.ORT_SEQUENTIAL
   so.graph_optimization_level = onnxruntime.GraphOptimizationLevel.ORT_ENABLE_ALL

   exproviders = ['CUDAExecutionProvider', 'CPUExecutionProvider']

   model_onnx_path = os.path.join(".", "resnet18.onnx")
   ort_session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession(model_onnx_path, so, providers=exproviders)

   options = ort_session.get_provider_options()
   cuda_options = options['CUDAExecutionProvider']
   cuda_options['cudnn_conv_use_max_workspace'] = '1'
   ort_session.set_providers(['CUDAExecutionProvider'], [cuda_options])

   #IOBinding
   input_names = ort_session.get_inputs()[0].name
   output_names = ort_session.get_outputs()[0].name
   io_binding = ort_session.io_binding()

   io_binding.bind_cpu_input(input_names, x)
   io_binding.bind_output(output_names, device)

   #warm up run
   ort_session.run_with_iobinding(io_binding)
   ort_outs = io_binding.copy_outputs_to_cpu()

   latency = []

   for i in range(total_samples):
      t0 = time.time()
      ort_session.run_with_iobinding(io_binding)
      latency.append(time.time() - t0)
      ort_outs = io_binding.copy_outputs_to_cpu()
   print('Number of runs:', len(latency))
   print("Average onnxruntime {} Inference time = {} ms".format(device.type, format(sum(latency) * 1000 / len(latency), '.2f')))

if __name__ == '__main__':
   torch.cuda.empty_cache()
   resnet = (models.resnet18(pretrained=True)).to(device=device)
   convert_to_onnx(resnet)
   infer_onnxruntime()
   infer_pytorch(resnet)
```

**Output**

If run on CPU,

```
Average onnxruntime cpu Inference time = 18.48 ms
Average PyTorch cpu Inference time = 51.74 ms
```

but, if run on GPU, I see

```
Average onnxruntime cuda Inference time = 47.89 ms
Average PyTorch cuda Inference time = 8.94 ms
```

If I change graph optimizations to onnxruntime.GraphOptimizationLevel.ORT\_DISABLE\_ALL, I see some improvements in inference time on GPU, but its still slower than Pytorch.

I use io binding for the input tensor numpy array and the nodes of the model are on GPU.

Further, during the processing for onnxruntime, I print device usage stats and I see this -

```
Using device: cuda:0
GPU Device name: Quadro M2000M
Memory Usage:
Allocated: 0.1 GB
Cached:    0.1 GB
```

So, GPU device is being used.

Further, I have used the resnet18.onnx model from the ModelZoo to see if it is a converted mode issue, but i get the same results.

What am I doing wrong or missing here?
